## Source-by-Source Evidence Notes

### ACTING-S001 — RADA BA Acting admissions
RADA’s current BA Acting page sets out a four-stage process: preliminary self-tape, second-round self-tape, short workshop, then full workshop day plus interview. The preliminary self-tape requires one classical speech, one contemporary speech, and a short spoken introduction. The second-round self-tape adds a different classical speech and a short unaccompanied song. RADA states that workshop stages are where the panel looks for imaginative response to text and character, physical and vocal adaptability, ability to take direction, and how the applicant works and observes in a group. The page also contains explicit disabled-applicant support language and equality language. This is strong evidence for later separation of tape-observable material from workshop-only evidence. citeturn26view0turn26view1turn26view4turn26view5

### ACTING-S002 — LAMDA BA Professional Acting
The BA Professional Acting course page mainly provides admissions framing, fees and a route to the audition-process page rather than detailed acting tasks. It is still useful as an official BA acting admissions source and as confirmation that audition structure is handled elsewhere in LAMDA’s admissions system. Treat this source as process / framing only in later synthesis. citeturn27view0

### ACTING-S003 — LAMDA audition process
LAMDA’s audition-process page is one of the strongest B1 sources for official self-tape acting evidence. It requires two contrasting monologues, one from LAMDA’s classical list and one contemporary speech, and states that LAMDA wants to see character choices and interpretation of the text, prepared without outside help or direction. The same page explicitly separates self-tapes from later in-person workshop and final recall stages, and includes inclusive audition-adjustment language. It also states that unsuccessful self-tape links are deleted and that self-tape feedback is not provided. citeturn27view3turn27view5turn27view6turn27view7turn28view0turn28view1turn28view3

### ACTING-S004 — Guildhall drama auditions
Guildhall’s drama-auditions route confirms a self-recorded first round followed by in-person later stages. Through the linked official acting-audition requirements content, Guildhall asks for an introduction and two monologues, one classical and one modern, and asks candidates to explain who they are, what they are performing and why they have chosen the pieces. The linked page also uses language about seeing candidates’ interests in the wider world and the context of the pieces, which is useful later for text/context evidence rather than generic praise. citeturn2view3turn8view0

### ACTING-S005 — Guildhall auditions and interviews
Guildhall’s school-wide auditions/interviews page explicitly says auditions are designed to assess attainment and potential. For Acting it confirms a three-stage process with a self-recorded first round and in-person second round and final recall. It also contains concrete disability-arrangements language, including reasonable adjustments and step-free room access where needed. This is a strong official source for potential-language and accessibility language in admissions. citeturn29view0turn29view2

### ACTING-S006 — Royal Central current BA Acting admissions page
Search results verified what appears to be the current Royal Central BA Acting audition-process page and related self-tape shot-options page, but the official pages themselves returned access errors in this run. Because the source could not be opened, it should be treated as inaccessible rather than extracted. The search snippets do, however, verify that current official acting-process and shot-options pages likely exist. citeturn30search0turn30search2turn30search6turn31view0turn31view1turn31view2

### ACTING-S007 — Royal Central official audition advice video
Official Royal Central audition-advice video/search snippets were located on the school’s YouTube presence, but the videos could not be opened reliably in this run. Use this only as fallback official guidance if S006 remains inaccessible in later work. Do not treat it as a substitute for the official admissions page without saying so explicitly. citeturn32search0turn32search2turn32search4

### ACTING-S008 — Bristol Old Vic Theatre School MFA Professional Acting
BOVTS’s MFA Professional Acting page gives clear admissions evidence. Preliminary auditions are online and require a verse speech from a classical English play, a prose piece from a 20th/21st-century play, and a short unaccompanied song. The panel looks for a high standard of acting, preparation, and ability to take direction. Successful applicants are then called for an in-person recall with the Head of Course. This is a useful official source for classical/modern contrast, direction-response language and the presence of song inside a professional-acting admissions pathway. citeturn34view0turn34view5

### ACTING-S009 — Royal Conservatoire of Scotland BA Acting
RCS provides unusually clear multi-round acting-audition evidence. First round is live in person or live online, not pre-recorded for this cycle. Applicants prepare either one modern speech plus one verse speech, or two modern speeches, each under two minutes, and the panel may redirect one piece. Round two becomes workshop-style, potentially using a short script sent in advance. Final recall asks for a new monologue and includes an interview. The page also includes explicit fair-access / fee-waiver language and disability-support links. citeturn36view0turn36view1turn37view0turn37view1turn37view2turn37view3

### ACTING-S010 — Royal Welsh acting admissions
The Royal Welsh Acting – Stage, Screen and Recorded Media page was URL-locked successfully, and the accessible rendering showed first-round audition, on-demand self-tape and recalls as active headings. However, the detailed content under those headings was not fully exposed in the retrieved version. This means the source can support that the programme distinguishes first-round and recall stages, and that self-tape is part of the process, but not yet the detailed acting-task content. citeturn13view0

### ACTING-S011 — Rose Bruford acting admissions
Rose Bruford’s acting course page confirms that offers may reflect future potential, not only formal tariff attainment, and points applicants to a distinct auditions page for the acting-process detail. The course page is also useful for its explicit stage / television / radio / screen framing, but it does not itself expose the acting-audition tasks in enough detail for full B1 extraction. citeturn38view0turn38view3turn38view4

### ACTING-S012 — Mountview acting course page
Mountview’s course page confirms that first-round BA Performance – Acting auditions are normally in person, with an online first-round option for international candidates and exceptional circumstances, and directs candidates to the detailed preparation page. It is therefore useful as an official process/framing source rather than a task-level acting-criteria source. citeturn35view0

### ACTING-S013 — Mountview what to prepare
Mountview’s preparation page contains explicit acting-task evidence. For BA Performance – Acting it asks for one prose speech from after 2000 and one verse speech from before 1800, each under two minutes, from published plays, close to the applicant’s age, and in the applicant’s own accent. It also says that online auditions include an additional filmed Physical Storytelling exercise, while in-person auditions may include redirection on the speeches. This is strong evidence for form distinctions, own-accent language and the separation between taped and in-person evidence. citeturn35view3turn35view4turn35view5

### ACTING-S014 — ArtsEd auditions
ArtsEd’s audition page is a strong official acting self-tape source. For BA Acting, first round is online and requires two speeches, each up to two minutes, one from a modern play written after 1990 and one classical / heightened-language speech. ArtsEd explicitly says applicants can film on phones, that production value is not what the panel is looking for, and that candidates should use their natural or heritage voice. Its self-tape tips ask for steady camera, neutral background, private quiet space, simple lighting, mid-torso framing and off-camera eyeline during speeches, and say candidates should present the work as they would in an in-person audition rather than a “camera” audition. Recalls are in person. citeturn25view0turn25view1turn24view1turn24view2turn24view4turn24view5

### ACTING-S015 — ArtsEd BA Acting page
This row was not independently reopened in this run because S014 already carried the acting-audition evidence. It remains a follow-up source only if later synthesis needs course-framing language distinct from the main auditions page.

### ACTING-S016 — East 15 auditions
East 15’s top-level auditions page confirms that all auditioning applicants must submit a Round 1 video audition and that successful candidates are recalled for Round 2 on campus, at regional / international venues, or online. It is process evidence rather than detailed acting-task evidence, and works best alongside S017. citeturn11view7

### ACTING-S017 — East 15 preparing for auditions
East 15’s preparation page is one of the strongest B1 sources. It requires a short introduction, a contemporary speech, and a heightened-language speech, all in English, with explicit filming guidance. East 15 says a smartphone is sufficient, wants the speech delivered straight to the camera lens, asks for two different framings across the two speeches, cautions against getting too busy in the frame, wants one-take speeches, and requires a web-accessible upload format. It also explicitly says the school wants to see how the applicant can embody the role and make choices. citeturn18view0

### ACTING-S018 — Manchester apply & audition
Manchester’s apply-and-audition page confirms that audition is part of admissions for Acting and that there are no audition fees. It is useful as a process overview rather than a task-level acting source. citeturn16view7

### ACTING-S019 — Manchester BA Acting audition page
Manchester’s BA Acting page is strong acting-audition evidence. First round is a video link with a short introduction and either two contrasting monologues or a monologue plus a musical-theatre song. Video advice emphasises neutral background, direct address to the lens at points, simple clothing, good sound, and minimal editing. The page then explicitly says the school is looking for creative, committed, versatile, enthusiastic applicants and values authenticity, originality and depth. It also includes a disability-welcome statement. citeturn19view3turn19view5

### ACTING-S020 — Oxford School of Drama three-year acting
Oxford’s page is exceptionally detailed. It requires one self-tape link containing a close-up introduction explaining the applicant’s choices and reasons for training there, followed by a waist-up contemporary speech and a contrasting second speech, which may be contemporary, classical, or spoken word. The page specifies eyeline to the side of camera for speeches. First recall then requires two speeches, including a classical option if not already shown; recalls involve group workshop, redirection, later unseen text, and closer work with panel members. Oxford also explicitly says it wants to see collaboration, creativity and craft, and notes that a foundation-course offer may be made at recall. citeturn20view0turn20view1turn17view12turn17view13turn20view5

### ACTING-S021 — National Youth Theatre auditions
NYT is not a higher-education conservatoire source, but it does provide explicit acting-audition language. Applicants prepare a short monologue from a play, film or TV show. NYT says auditioners look for use of vocal range, physical approach and quality, emotional connection to text, and approach to working with others / ensemble. It also includes barrier-reduction language and references both self-tape and recall result pathways. This is useful later as a supplementary comparator, not as a sole standard. citeturn21view0turn21view2turn21view3turn21view4

### ACTING-S022 — Juilliard drama admissions
Juilliard’s BFA Acting page clearly separates remote prescreen from live audition and callbacks. Applicants prepare four memorised monologues in total, with two heightened-text and two contemporary pieces ready; the initial live audition usually asks for one heightened-text and one contemporary piece. Callbacks may involve additional monologues, a cappella singing, cold readings, group exercises, improvisation and interviews. Juilliard’s decision language explicitly refers to “potential and artistry”, which is important later for training-potential handling. citeturn16view13turn16view14turn17view9turn17view10turn17view11

### ACTING-S023 — Yale acting application requirements
Yale’s application-requirements page is useful for formal process boundaries. It states that all acting applicants who meet degree requirements must audition in person according to the schedule, and that only one application and one audition are permitted per cycle. It also frames the course as advanced acting training at MFA / certificate level. citeturn16view17turn22view8turn22view9

### ACTING-S024 — Yale acting auditions
Yale’s audition page is a strong live-stage acting source. Applicants present two contrasting memorised audition pieces, fully memorised, totalling no more than five minutes, and are advised to be ready with additional material. Callback stages may include physical and vocal warm-up, a cappella singing, working on prepared monologues with committee members, and interview activity. Final callback sessions then include classes, faculty contact and fuller school immersion. This is strong evidence for what Yale treats as later-stage rather than initial presentation evidence. citeturn22view2turn22view4turn22view5turn22view6

### ACTING-S025 — NYU Tisch drama artistic review
The acting artistic-review page and parent admissions page were URL-locked successfully, but the detailed acting-task requirements were only partly exposed in this run. What is clear is that Tisch maintains a distinct acting artistic-review route and that, for regular decision acting applicants, an additional video submission requirement was introduced on the parent how-to-apply page. This justifies keeping NYU as an official but partial B1 source for later follow-up. citeturn16view15turn16view16

### ACTING-S026 — Carnegie Mellon undergraduate drama admission
CMU provides exceptionally clear prescreen/live distinctions. Acting applicants submit a prescreen with two contrasting monologues, one classical with heightened language and one contemporary, from published plays rather than musicals. Prescreen files must be separate, include slates, use ordinary available technology, and use specified ½-body and ¾- or full-body framings. Invited auditions then repeat the classical/contemporary contrast live or virtually, may request a third monologue, and expect applicants to have read the full play so they can show understanding of character and situation. citeturn23view3turn23view5turn23view6

### ACTING-S027 — USC BFA Acting for Stage and Screen
USC’s BFA Acting for Stage and Screen page is one of the clearest official shot-language sources. Applicants upload two separately filmed monologues, one classical and one contemporary, each memorised and performed in the context of the whole play. USC specifies that the contemporary monologue should be a close-up and the classical piece a full-body shot, requires clear sound and understandable audio, asks for a natural voice without accent or dialect, and forbids costumes. This is strong width-of-frame and natural-voice evidence, though it is still an admissions source rather than a complete screen-acting descriptor framework. citeturn16view20turn17view0turn17view1

## Reusable Handoff Pack for ACTING-B2 and Later ACTING-SYN

### ACTING-B1 handoff summary

ACTING-B1 has produced a usable official-admissions evidence base for later Acting synthesis. The strongest coverage is now in multi-stage audition structure, first-round submission requirements, text-type distinctions and the boundary between what schools ask to see on tape or in initial audition and what they reserve for workshops, recalls, callbacks and interviews. Across RADA, LAMDA, Guildhall, RCS, ArtsEd, East 15, Manchester, Oxford, Juilliard, Yale, Carnegie Mellon and USC, the evidence consistently shows that acting admissions are not treated as one generic presentation standard. Instead, schools repeatedly structure auditions through contrasting speeches or monologues, usually with some form of classical / verse / heightened-text and contemporary distinction, and then use later stages to test redirection, group work, unseen text, interviews, songs, movement tasks or wider flexibility.

B1 also now gives a strong official base for acting self-tape assessability. ArtsEd, East 15, Manchester, Oxford, Carnegie Mellon and USC all provide usable evidence on sound, light, framing, eyeline, edit limits, neutral backgrounds, smartphone acceptability and simple capture. That evidence does not yet amount to a complete screen-acting rubric, but it is already enough to show that later Acting outputs must separate technical readability from acting quality and must not reward production polish as talent evidence.

The other major gain is evidence around speech and voice inside acting admissions. Multiple official sources ask for the candidate’s natural voice, own accent or everyday speaking voice, and several sources care about whether the applicant can communicate text clearly and in context. That will matter later because TapeCoach still routes spoken acting voice through the stored vocal field, so later audit and revision will need to contain that semantics risk without turning spoken acting into singing language.

The main unresolved items are narrow and non-blocking. Royal Central’s current acting admissions pages were verified by search but remained access-blocked; Royal Welsh exposed only partial admissions detail in the retrievable rendering; NYU Tisch’s acting artistic-review detail was only partly exposed; and Rose Bruford’s acting page needs separate acting-audition-page follow-up if later synthesis needs more than course framing. None of those issues block progression to B2.

### Compact provisional findings list

- **ACTING-B1-F01**: official acting admissions commonly separate tape / initial audition evidence from workshop / callback / interview evidence
- **ACTING-B1-F02**: contrasting speeches / monologues, often classical-plus-contemporary, are the dominant official acting ask
- **ACTING-B1-F03**: schools repeatedly expect title / character / playwright / full-play context knowledge
- **ACTING-B1-F04**: official self-tape guidance prioritises assessability and simple capture over production polish
- **ACTING-B1-F05**: natural voice / own accent language recurs in official acting admissions
- **ACTING-B1-F06**: direction response, group work, unseen text and broader flexibility are mainly later-stage evidence
- **ACTING-B1-F07**: official admissions language mixes current attainment with future potential
- **ACTING-B1-F08**: accessibility, adjustments and fair-access language are already visible in B1
- **ACTING-B1-F09**: screen / shot / framing specificity appears, but full screen-acting criteria remain thin in B1
- **ACTING-B1-F10**: some acting admissions routes include songs or hybrid tasks, so later acting-only work must preserve boundaries

### ACTING-B1 extraction limitations

- B1 is strongest on admissions process and what schools ask candidates to prepare; it is weaker on formal acting-descriptor language.
- Screen-acting criteria are still thinner than self-tape logistics.
- Comedy, physical theatre, duologue / reader relationship and methodology-neutral acting descriptors remain undercovered in B1.
- Accessibility language is present, but B4 will still be needed to complete inclusive-assessment coverage.
- Royal Central and partial-access sources must remain explicit limitations, not silently treated as resolved.

### What B1 now covers well

- Official acting admissions structure
- First-round submission requirements
- Classical / contemporary and verse / prose distinctions
- Self-tape framing / eyeline / simple-capture expectations
- Natural voice / own accent signals
- Recall / callback / workshop boundaries
- Admissions-language use of potential
- Early accessibility and fair-access evidence

### What must be picked up in B2, B3 and B4

- **B2**: screen acting, self-tape performance specificity, stage vs screen naturalism, classical / contemporary text handling beyond admissions logistics, duologue / reader relationship, comedy, physical theatre
- **B3**: practitioner, casting and methodology-neutral acting language; professional self-tape and casting expectations; live-room versus finished-tape boundaries from industry sources
- **B4**: accessibility, disability / neurodiversity, anti-bias casting and audition guidance, and targeted gap-fills where B1 and B2 remain thin

## Source-by-Source Evidence Notes

**ACTING-S029 — LAMDA Exams Acting**  
The public exam page and the 2024 syllabus explicitly frame acting as a performance qualification built around interpretive skills, technical skills and knowledge of process. The acting exam is available in solo, duologue and combined formats, with solo exams available online. The syllabus requires memorised scenes and, by level, moves from basic character/location questions to more advanced demands around text and subtext, character intentions and objectives, vocal control, diction, physical response, context and period/style understanding. It also permits some medium crossover: own-choice material can include published plays and feature films at several levels, while higher levels restrict own-choice scenes to post-1980 plays or feature films and explicitly exclude television serials and novel adaptations. The same syllabus also includes named-practitioner knowledge at higher levels, so it is useful as a descriptor source but must not be universalised into one acting-method standard. citeturn0view0turn11view0turn11view1turn11view2turn11view3turn11view4turn11view5turn13view0turn17view2

**ACTING-S030 — Trinity Acting**  
The public page and specification frame acting as a drama qualification centred on vocal, physical and characterisation skills, with solo, duo, group and digital options. Trinity’s acting specification distinguishes task types rather than treating acting as one undifferentiated performance event: monologues, duologues, original scenes and reflections are separate components. It also requires contrast by language style, genre and/or period at some grades, expects work from published sources unless stated otherwise, and at intermediate/advanced levels requires acting play extracts to come from theatre rather than film or television. The reflection component is important: candidates may be assessed on context, rehearsal process, voice/body choices, writing styles, contrast, pair collaboration and interpretation. That makes Trinity highly useful for separating tape-observable performance from non-performance knowledge, but it also means later Acting outputs should not imply that every contextual claim can be inferred from the finished tape alone. citeturn21view1turn9view0turn9view1turn9view2turn13view5turn13view6turn17view3turn17view4turn18view0turn18view1turn18view3turn18view4turn18view5

**ACTING-S031 — Trinity Acting for Screen**  
The accessible public source family provides explicit screen-specific evidence. The overview page says every performance task integrates eyeline and camera framing, and it identifies separate screen demands: full-body framing, close-up expression, direct-to-camera ident, dialogue with read-in lines, a listening task built around non-verbal reaction, reflective review, smartphone-or-camera filming and no editing required. The resources page makes the framing pattern even more concrete: wide shot for Ident, close-up for Monologue and Listening, and mid-shot for Dialogue and Playback Review. This is one of the strongest B2 anchors for maintaining a genuine screen-acting layer in later synthesis. The limitation is that the linked guide/syllabus were not equally retrievable in full public text from this run, so later stages should stay within publicly surfaced task language unless a fuller official source is extracted. citeturn21view0turn12view0turn10view0

**ACTING-S032 — Spotlight self-tape essentials**  
This article is professional guidance rather than a formal assessment framework, but it contains high-value observable boundaries. It supports smartphone capture, recommends landscape filming, plain backgrounds, eye-level camera placement, minimal background noise, soft forward lighting, reader use, eyeline kept close to camera, mid-close framing by default, limited props and costume, and restraint on repeated takes. It also says to read instructions carefully and follow task-specific requests, including whether an ident is needed. The source is particularly useful for separating assessability from production polish: the article contains equipment suggestions, but its core guidance is about making the work readable, not about rewarding expensive kit. That should inform later specificity and fairness language, not become hard scoring criteria. citeturn19view0turn19view1turn19view2turn19view3turn19view4

**ACTING-S033 — RADA self-tape guide PDF**  
This is a concise but very useful official setup document. It prioritises one thing above all else: the panel must be able to see and hear the performer clearly. It explicitly says no specialist equipment is needed, phone capture is acceptable, landscape framing is required, a plain background is preferred, quiet rooms improve voice clarity, and costumes/props are unnecessary. It also gives task structure: start wide, then if possible move to a mid shot, state the three pieces being performed and why they were chosen, and perform two classical speeches plus one contemporary speech. It instructs candidates not to look straight down the lens during speeches but to place the eyeline slightly to the side as if speaking to another character. It further discourages excessive retakes and closes with a clear anti-polish message: do not overthink it; they want to see the real person. Because this document is tied to a specific RADA course and includes a song task, later synthesis must use it as a self-tape/text-type anchor rather than as a universal acting-only rulebook. citeturn16view0turn16view1turn16view2turn17view1

**ACTING-S034 — Spotlight performer self-tape guide**  
This source family was correctly completed as process-only. The represented and self-represented performer pages explain how requests are received, where the performer sees instructions, how due dates and statuses are displayed, how to accept or decline a request, and how uploads work. They also note that once a tape is submitted it cannot be edited or deleted, that self-represented performers cannot submit via the app, and which file formats the platform accepts. That makes this source relevant to self-tape workflow and to the distinction between performance guidance and platform admin, but it does not supply acting-form, text-type or performance-criteria language. It should therefore be kept in the handoff as a workflow boundary source, not promoted into scoring language later. citeturn20view0turn20view1turn20view2turn20view3turn20view4turn20view5

## Provisional B2 Findings

**ACTING-B2-F01**  
Formal B2 sources do not treat acting as one generic standard. General acting frameworks and screen-acting frameworks are separated at source level: the acting specifications focus on vocal, physical and characterisation skills across monologue, duologue and staged extracts, while the screen framework adds camera-framing, eyeline, dialogue-with-read-ins, listening and direct-to-camera ident tasks.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S029, ACTING-S030, ACTING-S031  
- **Source type:** Formal assessment framework  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** Stage/general acting, monologue, duologue, screen acting, self-tape  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Both  
- **Evidence confidence:** High  
- **Why it matters later:** It directly supports later subtype-specific Acting language and blocks a single flattened acting standard.  
- **Caution:** Trinity Screen gives the clearest screen-task structure, but it is still a qualification source rather than a professional casting rubric. citeturn11view0turn21view1turn21view0turn12view0

**ACTING-B2-F02**  
Camera relationship is task-dependent rather than universal. Trinity Screen requires direct address in the Ident task, uses read-in lines for Dialogue, and assigns different frame sizes by task; RADA tells candidates not to look straight down the lens for speeches; Spotlight places eyeline close to camera unless instructions say otherwise.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S031, ACTING-S032, ACTING-S033  
- **Source type:** Formal screen framework; professional self-tape guidance; official conservatoire self-tape guidance  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** Screen acting, self-tape, monologue/speech, dialogue  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Tape-observable  
- **Evidence confidence:** High  
- **Why it matters later:** Later Acting outputs will need task-aware eyeline wording, not a single blanket rule.  
- **Caution:** Some variation is source-family and task specific; do not convert it into one universal eyeline metric. citeturn21view0turn12view0turn19view1turn16view1

**ACTING-B2-F03**  
B2 gives strong evidence that self-tape assessability should prioritise clear sight and sound, simple framing, readable domestic capture and restraint on props/costume/retakes rather than production polish. Smartphone capture is explicitly acceptable in both Trinity Screen and RADA sources, and Spotlight’s guidance is likewise built around practical readability rather than elaborate production.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S031, ACTING-S032, ACTING-S033  
- **Source type:** Formal screen framework; professional self-tape guidance; official conservatoire self-tape guidance  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** Self-tape across acting forms  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Tape-observable  
- **Evidence confidence:** High  
- **Why it matters later:** This will be central to later assessability wording and anti-polish guardrails.  
- **Caution:** Spotlight includes gear preferences that should not become scoring rules. citeturn21view0turn19view0turn19view2turn16view0turn16view1turn17view1

**ACTING-B2-F04**  
Voice and speech are clearly treated here as acting evidence rather than singing evidence. Across LAMDA and Trinity acting specifications, the recurring markers are audibility, clarity of diction, vocal control, modulation, pace, pitch, volume and vocal response to text/character.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S029, ACTING-S030  
- **Source type:** Formal assessment framework  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** General acting, monologue, duologue, stage acting  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Both  
- **Evidence confidence:** High  
- **Why it matters later:** It provides a direct source base for containing the reused `vocal` field to speech/voice-delivery meaning in acting contexts, without drifting into singing language.  
- **Caution:** Some voice-related evidence in these frameworks is coupled with reflection/Q&A rather than raw performance alone. citeturn11view0turn11view2turn9view1turn13view6

**ACTING-B2-F05**  
Context and preparation knowledge are often assessed separately from the performed extract. LAMDA uses examiner questions about character feeling, location, objective, role in the whole play and author/style influences; Trinity uses reflection on material, rehearsal process, style, voice/body techniques and pair collaboration.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S029, ACTING-S030  
- **Source type:** Formal assessment framework  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** General acting, monologue, duologue/pair acting  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Both  
- **Evidence confidence:** High  
- **Why it matters later:** It strongly supports a later boundary between what a tape shows and what must not be overclaimed unless directly evidenced or separately provided.  
- **Caution:** These are exam structures, not identical to audition structures, but the boundary remains highly relevant. citeturn11view1turn11view2turn9view2turn13view6

**ACTING-B2-F06**  
Text-type and medium boundaries matter, but not identically across sources. Trinity Acting keeps acting extracts tied to theatre and period/language-style contrast, while LAMDA’s acting syllabus permits feature-film material in some acting contexts and sets different restrictions at advanced levels. RADA’s self-tape guide explicitly separates classical and contemporary speeches.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S029, ACTING-S030, ACTING-S033  
- **Source type:** Formal assessment framework; official conservatoire self-tape guidance  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** General acting, stage acting, speech/monologue, text-type handling  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Both  
- **Evidence confidence:** High  
- **Why it matters later:** Later synthesis must not force one uniform classical/contemporary/stage/screen rule across all Acting subdomains.  
- **Caution:** These are task frameworks, not one universal industry hierarchy of text types. citeturn13view0turn18view1turn18view3turn16view1

**ACTING-B2-F07**  
The screen-specific source family is strong on framing, listening, dialogue rhythm and direct-to-camera address, but weaker on publicly exposed comparative wording about stage versus screen naturalism.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S031  
- **Source type:** Formal screen framework  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** Screen acting, self-tape  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Tape-observable  
- **Evidence confidence:** Medium  
- **Why it matters later:** It supports screen-specific wording, but it also warns against overstating stronger stage-vs-screen theory than the accessible public source actually spells out.  
- **Caution:** More nuanced comparison language will likely need B3 practitioner sources rather than B2 alone. citeturn21view0turn12view0turn10view0

**ACTING-B2-F08**  
ACTING-S034 is operationally useful but evaluatively empty. It draws a clean boundary between self-tape platform workflow and acting-performance assessment.  
- **Supported by source IDs:** ACTING-S034  
- **Source type:** Platform workflow guidance  
- **Acting forms / context affected:** All self-tape contexts  
- **Tape-observable / live-room / both:** Neither as an acting criterion source

Accessibility-safe and anti-bias evidence in B2 is present mostly as soft fairness and anti-polish boundaries, not as a full accessibility framework. The deeper access spine still belongs to B4.

## Reusable Handoff Pack for ACTING-B3 and Later ACTING-SYN

**ACTING-B2 handoff summary**

ACTING-B2 has now completed the form-specific extraction layer that B1 was missing. The strongest gain is that there is now a credible public-source basis for treating general acting and screen acting as related but non-identical assessment contexts. The general formal frameworks, especially LAMDA Exams and Trinity Acting, emphasise vocal, physical and characterisation skills, interpretive choices, context and reflection across monologue, duologue and range-of-style work. By contrast, Trinity Acting for Screen adds task-specific screen evidence: eyeline, frame adaptation, direct-to-camera ident work, dialogue with read-in lines, non-verbal listening and filmed playback review. This means later Acting synthesis no longer has to infer a screen layer from admissions logistics alone. citeturn11view0turn21view1turn21view0turn12view0

B2 also materially strengthens the assessability spine. Spotlight’s self-tape essentials and RADA’s self-tape guide both prioritise readable sound, clear framing, plain backgrounds, limited props/costume, manageable domestic capture and restraint on repeated takes. RADA is especially useful because it combines simple-capture guidance with explicit acting text-type asks: two classical speeches and one contemporary speech, framed first wide and then, if possible, at mid shot, with the eyeline placed slightly off lens. Together with Trinity Screen’s task-specific framing, this is enough to support later work on camera relationship, screen-specific observability and anti-polish guardrails without importing production-value bias. citeturn19view0turn19view1turn16view0turn16view1turn21view0turn12view0

A third important gain is semantic clarity around spoken acting voice. Both LAMDA and Trinity repeatedly treat speech evidence as audibility, clarity, diction, modulation, pace, pitch, volume and response to the text or character, not singing. They also make visible a crucial claim-scope boundary: some evidence sits in separate questions or reflections about context, objective, rehearsal and interpretation rather than in the performed extract itself. That will matter later when the Acting branch addresses the reused `vocal` field and the risk of overclaiming from finished tapes. citeturn11view0turn11view1turn11view2turn9view1turn9view2

The remaining B2 limitations are clear. Comedy and physical-theatre criteria remain thin. Publicly exposed stage-versus-screen naturalism language is thinner than task-specific screen framing. Accessibility-specific acting-assessment evidence is not yet complete and must still be picked up in B4. ACTING-S034 should be preserved as process-only workflow context, not promoted into rubric wording. citeturn21view0turn10view0turn20view0turn20view2

**4. Source-by-Source Evidence Notes**

**ACTING-S035 — Equity self-tape & Zoom guidance**

The source explicitly frames itself as best-practice guidance for scripted-drama self-tapes and Zoom auditions. It says casting should give performers as much information as possible at request stage, including tone, style, period and, where possible, a brief sense of the director’s or lead creative’s vision. It treats simplicity as central: performers should not normally be asked to provide their own props or re-arrange their home as if it were a set. It also sets explicit fair-process boundaries: a four-day minimum turnaround for most self-tapes, a three-day minimum where the request is three pages or fewer, a six-page cap for a first self-tape, limits on the number of roles, scenes and versions requested, and specific weekend / Bank Holiday due-date rules. Readers are described as beneficial but not mandatory, and performers are not expected to pay for them. Translation responsibility is placed on production, not the performer, when the script needs significant translation. The page also says performers should not be asked to self-tape fully or partially nude and that casting should only request as many self-tapes as can actually be considered. The access section adds explicit inclusive-process language: Word rather than PDF documents, BSL interpreter responsibility, extra preparation time, asking all auditionees about access requirements, practical adjustments around fatigue, lighting, guides, step-free access and access-worker scheduling. No acting method is privileged. This is a strong B3 source, but it is still chiefly a process and fairness document, not a direct acting-descriptor framework. citeturn1view0

**ACTING-S036 — SAG-AFTRA self-tape guidelines**

The named member-guidance page publicly surfaces as a portal to new contract bulletins, but the page itself was blocked to direct fetch in this environment. Official SAG-AFTRA search exposure and linked official TV/theatrical materials nonetheless make several process rules explicit: breakdowns, sides and/or scripts are to be provided at least 48 hours before submission deadlines, excluding weekends and holidays; minors receive 72 hours; first self-tapes are capped at eight industry-standard pages and second or later self-tapes at twelve; performers cannot be required to memorise and may hold sides or use a prompting device; performers must be given the option of a live virtual or in-person audition instead of a self-tape; and producers cannot require a resolution above 720p, a non-free upload site, editing software or specific equipment. The same official materials also surface privacy and safety constraints: self-tapes must be stored securely, cannot be made public without performer consent, and self-tapes cannot require nudity or stunts. Method language is absent. The later caution is important: this is excellent contractual and burden-boundary evidence, but later stages must not mistake contractual process rules for direct acting-quality descriptors. citeturn0search1turn15search1turn15search2turn10search0turn9search0turn10search17turn16search1turn8search2

**ACTING-S037 — SAG-AFTRA self-tape anatomy**

The named article is publicly traceable but direct fetch was blocked and public exposure is thin. The publicly exposed official snippets still show what kind of source it is: a practitioner/process article from SAG-AFTRA Magazine which emphasises that self-taping adds labour beyond audition preparation itself because performers must prepare, set up the space, record and sometimes edit the work. The article also highlights one of the medium differences between recorded and in-person auditions: sides or cue cards are more readily accessible in self-tapes. The exposed wording also frames a self-made tape as potentially the only chance a decision-maker has to see the performer. That is useful later as process-context evidence about mediated audition conditions and overclaim risk, but the public exposure here is too thin for direct rubric language. No robust acting criteria, access rules, or methodology language are sufficiently exposed from this source in this environment, so it is correctly treated as process-only. citeturn0search2turn7search0turn12search0turn14search0

## What B3 adds beyond formal frameworks, plus coverage and URL notes

**8. Practitioner / Professional Criteria Missing from Formal Frameworks**

B3 adds several things that B1 and B2 did not fully cover. The most important additions are explicit fair-process limits: how much material may reasonably be requested, how much time performers should have, what happens around weekends and holidays, and what cannot be shifted onto performers as unpaid labour or personal cost. Equity also adds reader handling, translation responsibility and explicit context-provision duties, while SAG-AFTRA adds contract-side guardrails on memorisation, paid platforms, specific equipment, resolution ceilings, secure storage, public-release consent and live virtual or in-person alternatives to self-tapes. Those are not acting descriptors, but they are crucial guardrails for later synthesis because they define what must not be treated as talent evidence. ACTING-S037 adds a narrower but still useful professional insight: self-taping is extra labour and a mediated format, with easier access to sides or cue cards than in the room, so later stages must separate process burden from performance evidence. citeturn1view0turn15search1turn15search2turn10search0turn9search0turn10search17turn16search1turn8search2turn14search0

## B4 decision and reusable handoff pack

**11. B4 Decision**

**ACTING-B4 appears required.**

**Rationale**  
B3 strengthens professional fairness, burden and anti-polish boundaries, and Equity adds meaningful access-process guidance. But B3 does not complete the gaps already carried forward from B1 and B2. In the material actually extracted here, disability-specific acting assessment, neurodiversity-specific guidance, visual-impairment-specific audition handling beyond general access, anti-bias casting language, and undercovered form-specific evidence such as physical theatre remain materially underdeveloped. Equity’s access section is valuable, but it is not enough on its own to stand in for the ScreenSkills, Graeae, Equity visual-impairment and form-gap B4 sources that were explicitly queued for this purpose. citeturn1view0turn14search0

**Evidence gaps driving the decision**
- accessibility-safe acting and speech assessment is still incomplete
- disability / neurodiversity / visual-impairment guidance is still incomplete
- anti-bias casting or audition guidance is still incomplete
- physical theatre / embodied acting evidence is still incomplete
- comedy remains undercovered
- methodology-neutral positive descriptor language remains thinner than needed

**Is missing evidence essential before ACTING-SYN?**  
Yes, especially for accessibility, anti-deficit handling and the remaining undercovered form-specific areas.

**Can any gap be carried into synthesis as a limitation instead of requiring B4?**  
A few thinner areas, such as comedy, could in theory be carried as explicit synthesis limitations. Accessibility-safe acting and speech assessment should not be left that thin before ACTING-SYN.

**Was the B4 ledger supplied?**  
Yes.

**12. Reusable Handoff Pack for ACTING-B4 or Later ACTING-SYN**

**ACTING-B3 handoff summary**

ACTING-B3 has now added the professional and union process layer that B1 and B2 did not fully cover. The biggest gain is explicit fairness and burden evidence around self-tapes. Equity’s scripted-drama self-tape and Zoom guidance gives clear process guardrails: casting should provide contextual information such as tone, style, period and creative vision where possible; requests should remain simple rather than asking performers to re-dress their homes as sets; turnaround and page burden should be proportionate; readers are beneficial but not mandatory and performers should not have to pay for them; and nude self-tapes should not be requested. Equity also adds the strongest explicit accessible-audition language seen so far in the Acting branch, including editable document format, interpreter responsibility, extra preparation time, universal access-requirement questions and practical adjustments for fatigue, lighting, step-free access and access-worker scheduling. citeturn1view0

SAG-AFTRA adds a different but equally useful layer: contract-side rules that prevent self-tape burdens from being mistaken for acting skill. In the official public exposure available here, the member-guidance page and linked TV/theatrical materials surface minimum time windows, page ceilings, a no-memorisation rule, live virtual or in-person alternatives to self-tapes, limits on technical demands, secure storage requirements, public-release consent limits and no-nudity / no-stunt boundaries. That is especially valuable for later non-regression work because it gives the Acting branch a strong source basis for separating performance evidence from production burden, upload friction, expensive equipment and privacy/safety issues. citeturn15search1turn15search2turn10search0turn9search0turn10search17turn16search1turn8search2

The remaining limitation is clear. The publicly exposed SAG-AFTRA “Self-Tape Anatomy” material is helpful as practitioner process context, especially in treating self-taping as extra labour and a mediated format in which sides or cue cards are more readily available, but it is too thinly exposed to serve as direct rubric language. More importantly, B3 does not remove the need for B4. Accessibility-safe acting assessment, disability/neurodiversity/visual-impairment handling, anti-bias guidance and undercovered form-specific gaps still need the queued B4 sources. citeturn14search0turn1view0

## Source-by-source evidence notes

**ACTING-S038 — ScreenSkills accessible audition standard**  
This standard explicitly treats accessible audition design as barrier-identification and barrier-removal work. It tells productions to identify barriers in the audition process and venue, confirm access requirements, adapt the process or location where needed, and respond to known requirements. Its scope is broader than step-free entry: it names environment, lighting, sound, transport, physical contact, personal space, timeframes and sensitivities, and it lists concrete resources such as braille printing, text-to-speech software, adaptive hardware, support workers, interpreters and support animals. The glossary is strongly anti-deficit: disability is framed through social barriers and attitudes rather than impairment, and the overview explicitly says accessible audition work should “encourage incidental casting”. There is no direct acting-performance descriptor layer here, and no direct tape criterion beyond access factors such as sound and lighting. citeturn7view0turn7view1turn7view5turn4view12turn4view14turn7view3

**ACTING-S039 — ScreenSkills access coordinator skills**  
This page adds an access-first production and casting layer rather than a performance-evaluation layer. It explicitly covers recruitment, casting, filming, editing and release, and says access coordinators should be embedded early so that solutions are built in from the outset. The page names deaf, disabled and/or neurodivergent talent directly, sets out the four pillars of access as physical, sensory, communication and cognitive, and requires confidentiality, access passports/riders, accessible materials, accessible schedule/location updates and sourcing of Easy Reads, interpreters, support workers and accessible travel. A particularly important non-deficit line is that the access coordinator’s work should allow talent to focus on their role rather than their own advocacy. This is highly relevant to fairness, but it is still not a direct acting-descriptor source. citeturn2view0turn8view0turn8view1turn5view0

**ACTING-S040 — Graeae access guidance**  
Graeae’s page is the strongest B4 source for social-model language and anti-deficit framing. It says access is central to the organisation’s work, explains that disabled and neurodivergent people are disabled by barriers rather than by impairment, rejects the medical-model framing that people need to be “fixed”, and places responsibility on organisations to make adaptations and adjustments. It also shows practical access culture: bespoke access solutions, accessible/alternative formats, access consultancy, access riders, BSL, audio description, captioning, audio flyers and Easy Read materials. The page is valuable because it shows access features as integral to creative practice rather than as add-ons, but it does not provide acting-performance criteria or audition-specific descriptors. citeturn2view2turn2view3turn12view1turn12view5

**ACTING-S041 — Equity advice for visually impaired actors**  
This is the most specific B4 source for how an audition or work process should adapt for visually impaired actors. It warns against treating visual impairment as monolithic, says preferred terms should be checked with the individual, and then gives concrete audition guidance: ask how the actor wants to access scripts, provide materials well in advance, avoid PDFs, use editable Word documents, use large clear type, consider line-feeding or recordings, offer an access worker in workshop auditions, use descriptive rather than demonstrative directions, and support orientation to buildings, rooms, crews and sets. It also recommends clear verbal instructions and notes trip hazards on set. Crucially, it explicitly encourages incidental casting of visually impaired and other disabled actors, without turning the role into a disability-only brief. The page is condition-specific, but it is highly valuable for anti-assumption and non-deficit handling. citeturn8view2turn6view0turn6view1turn5view5

**ACTING-S042 — East 15 Acting and Contemporary Theatre**  
This page is not an accessibility framework. Its B4 value lies in contemporary/creative/physical form coverage. It describes a course built around European physical theatre, character development, creativity, actor/writer-musician-choreographer identities, film, devising, writing, physical expression, clown, Shakespeare, parody, short film, physical comedy and site-specific classical work. It also names observation, self-assessment, reflection, research, improvisation, character studies and reacting to emotional upheaval through varied texts. These are useful signals for later synthesis because they widen the acting-form map beyond classical/contemporary speeches alone. However, the page is overtly methodology-shaped, naming Stanislavski, Commedia dell’Arte and Gaulier, and it is a course-description page rather than an audition or regulated assessment framework. citeturn13view2turn11view0turn3view0turn5view9

**ACTING-S043 — East 15 Acting and Fight Performance**  
This page provides the clearest B4 evidence for embodied acting and specialist physical performance. It frames the course around physical dramatic action, stage combat and performance, martial arts, gymnastics, weapons systems, movement, acrobatics, tumbling, dance, choreography, story and character action within a stage fight, fights for film, scenes for camera, devised work and audition technique. It also shows that the form can involve different presentational demands across venues and briefs. That is useful gap-fill evidence for embodied and fight-based acting contexts. But the same page makes its limits very clear: it is a specialist course, it assumes strenuous physical demands and a possible physical background, and it explicitly draws on Stanislavski plus inside-out and outside-in approaches. None of that can be universalised into a default acting standard. citeturn13view0turn2view8turn3view3turn5view10turn5view13

**Coverage and Gap Summary**

ACTING-B4 covers all six ledger rows, and all six reached a final extraction status of **fully extracted: criteria found**. No B4 source finished as no-relevant-criteria, process-only, duplicate/superseded, inaccessible or provenance-unclear. The strongest B4 evidence is in access-process design, social-model and anti-deficit language, visual-impairment-specific audition handling, accessible materials, communication access, and the separation of adaptation from acting quality. citeturn7view0turn7view1turn8view1turn8view2turn2view3

By topic, B4 is strongest in accessibility and fairness guidance across ACTING-S038 to ACTING-S041. It is moderate in anti-bias and incidental-casting language, because those ideas are present but not developed through a dedicated cross-industry bias framework. It is also moderate in physical and form-specific gap-fill because ACTING-S042 and ACTING-S043 expand the map for contemporary, embodied and fight-based acting, but they do so through school/course descriptors rather than through a neutral assessment framework. citeturn7view0turn8view1turn2view3turn13view2turn13view0

B4 remains thin in four areas that should be carried into ACTING-SYN as explicit limitations rather than treated as blockers: comedy, richer methodology-neutral positive acting descriptors, finer-grained neurodivergence-specific acting-assessment detail, and a fuller positive descriptor set for speech/voice under access conditions. Tape-observable versus live-room-only boundaries are now better protected on the access/process side, but B4 still does not create a direct performance rubric for those undercovered areas. On the evidence now in hand, ACTING-SYN can proceed, but it should do so **with explicit limitations**. citeturn5view9turn11view4turn8view1turn8view2turn13view2turn13view0

**ACTING-SYN Readiness Decision**

**ACTING-SYN ready with explicit limitations.**

The rationale is that B4 has now supplied the previously missing accessibility, visual-impairment handling, social-model and anti-deficit spine, while also adding enough partial evidence to map contemporary, embodied and fight-related acting forms without pretending they are already covered by generic acting guidance. The major blockers identified at the end of B3 are therefore no longer blockers. What remains are limitations: comedy is still too thin for strong rubric language; methodology-neutral positive acting descriptors remain thinner than ideal; neurodivergence-specific acting-assessment detail is broad rather than finely operationalised; and positive speech/voice descriptor language under access conditions is still lighter than the access-process layer around it. Those limits should be named in ACTING-SYN and not silently normalised away. citeturn7view1turn8view1turn8view2turn13view2turn13view0

## Reusable handoff and completion

**ACTING-B4 handoff summary**

ACTING-B4 has now completed the accessibility, fairness and gap-fill layer that remained incomplete after B1 to B3. The strongest gain is that the Acting branch now has a usable non-deficit access spine. ScreenSkills’ accessible-audition standard and access-coordinator guidance both frame access through barrier removal rather than impairment failure. Together they make clear that accessible acting assessment is not just about step-free entry: it can involve environment, lighting, sound, timing, personal space, information and communication barriers, access passports/riders, accessible materials, interpreters, support workers and confidential handling of access information. Just as importantly, ScreenSkills explicitly frames the work so that disabled, deaf and neurodivergent talent can focus on the role rather than on self-advocacy, and the accessible-audition standard explicitly encourages incidental casting. citeturn7view0turn7view1turn8view1

Graeae and Equity then sharpen the language and practice. Graeae provides the clearest social-model and anti-medical-model wording in the Acting source base so far, explicitly placing responsibility on organisations to make adaptations and adjustments for equality of access, and showing access features such as BSL, audio description, captioning, Easy Read and alternative formats as integral rather than peripheral. Equity’s visually impaired actors guidance is the most operational B4 source: editable scripts instead of PDFs, advance text, line-feeding, access workers, descriptive directing, clear verbal instructions, orientation to rooms and sets, and incidental casting without turning impairment into the whole role. That is enough to stop later synthesis from treating visual impairment, adaptation or communication support as acting deficits. citeturn2view3turn12view1turn8view2

B4 also adds partial form-gap evidence. East 15’s Acting and Contemporary Theatre page expands the map for devising, physical expressionism, clown, parody, short film, character studies and collaborative making. East 15’s Acting and Fight Performance page expands embodied and fight-based acting through stage combat, choreography, physical storytelling, fights for film and scenes for camera. These gains matter, but they come with a clear caution: both pages are specialist, school-shaped course descriptions with explicit methodology fingerprints, not universal acting-assessment standards. citeturn13view2turn13view0turn11view0turn5view10

The branch can now move to ACTING-SYN, but with explicit limitations. Comedy remains thin. Richer methodology-neutral positive acting descriptors remain thinner than ideal. Neurodivergence-specific acting-assessment detail is broader than it is operational. Speech/voice under access conditions is better covered as communication access than as a positive acting-descriptor set. Those limitations should be preserved in synthesis rather than treated as solved. citeturn5view9turn8view1turn8view2

- ACTING-B4-F01: access should be handled through barrier removal, not deficit inference
- ACTING-B4-F02: access requirements extend beyond mobility to communication, timing, environment, sound and support
- ACTING-B4-F03: fair access handling includes confidential access discussion, accessible materials and access riders/passports
- ACTING-B4-F04: visual-impairment-specific audition handling is now explicitly evidenced

\f1\b0\fs24 \cf0 Select 
\f0\b Voice / Singing
\f1\b0  as the next discipline branch.\
It is the highest-leverage next branch because the 
\f2\fs26 vocal
\f1\fs24  field is the most overloaded shared field in the current TapeCoach architecture: it means sung vocal for Song/MT, speech delivery for Acting/Monologue, and movement-technique proxy for Dance. That creates label, weighting and report-interpretation risk across every completed branch.\
Voice/Singing is also explicitly underdeveloped in the current baseline. The existing control sheet says Song/Voice already covers vocal performance, musical interpretation, acting/storytelling through song, audio clarity and brief adherence, but still lacks style-specific criteria for classical/legit, contemporary MT, belt, mix, pop/rock, jazz and folk, plus vocal-health/sustainability language, diction, resonance, passaggio, support, vibrato and stylistic authenticity.\
This also protects the MT anchor. Musical Theatre is currently the stabilised flow and must continue to show both Acting and Vocal where acting and singing are present; the current baseline also notes that MT acting-through-song is still implicit and that song feedback can over-focus on vocal technique rather than lyric/storytelling.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa298\partightenfactor0

\f0\b\fs36 \cf0 Why not Commercial next?\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f1\b0\fs24 \cf0 Commercial is important, but the current system already routes Commercial mainly through acting-as-presence/naturalism, brief, technical and audio. Its gap is subtype precision: to-camera, naturalistic screen, corporate/industrial and voiceover-style delivery. That is worth doing, but it is less foundational than cleaning up the true singing branch, because Voice/Singing affects Song, MT, label semantics, score interpretation and acting-through-song.\

## 4. Coverage Summary

**Counts**
- Total source rows identified: **43**
- Normalised active source count after excluding unresolved placeholder rows that should not be double-counted as active source families: **41**
- Count by assigned batch:
  - **ACTING-B1:** 28
  - **ACTING-B2:** 6
  - **ACTING-B3:** 3
  - **ACTING-B4:** 6
- Count by primary source type:
  - **Official admissions / conservatoire / drama-school:** 31
  - **Exam board / syllabus / formal assessment framework:** 3
  - **Professional body / union / casting-body guidance:** 3
  - **Accessibility / fairness / inclusion guidance:** 6

**Coverage by acting form / medium / text type**
- **Strong:** acting scene, monologue, screen/self-tape, staged recalls/workshops, classical / Shakespeare / heightened text, contemporary text, self-tape framing / eyeline / audibility.
- **Moderate:** duologue / reader relationship, stage versus screen handling, text understanding, objective/action/tactic language without explicit method lock-in, present-tape versus live-room-only distinctions.
- **Thinner / gap-watch:** comedy-specific criteria, physical-theatre-specific criteria, methodology-neutral language that is explicit rather than implied, class-coded polish / appearance exclusion language written specifically for acting rather than general self-tape practice.

**Coverage by assessment context**
- **Admissions / audition / recall / workshop:** dominant and well-covered.
- **Formal descriptor language:** present but concentrated in LAMDA Exams and Trinity.
- **Professional self-tape and fair-process guidance:** good coverage via Equity, Spotlight and SAG-AFTRA.
- **Accessibility / inclusive audition design:** solid early coverage via Equity, ScreenSkills and Graeae. citeturn22search1turn23search1turn37search3turn24search5turn34search1turn35search0turn38search0turn34search3turn34search0turn25search0turn26search0turn28search0turn28search9turn26search1turn29search1turn31search3turn31search0

## 5. Proposed Batch Plan

| Batch | Scope | Source count | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| ACTING-B1 | Official drama schools, conservatoires and admissions | 28 | Highest priority because official schools are strongest on audition structure, monologue/text asks, recall/workshop processes, training-potential language and what candidates are explicitly asked to show |
| ACTING-B2 | Acting forms, self-tape, screen/stage and text-type guidance | 6 | Anchored by LAMDA Exams, Trinity Acting, Trinity Acting for Screen, Spotlight and RADA self-tape guidance |
| ACTING-B3 | Practitioner, casting, professional and methodology-neutral guidance | 3 | Smaller but high-value batch focused on self-tape practice, process fairness and professional expectations |
| ACTING-B4 | Accessibility, fairness, methodology, form-specific and gap-fill sources | 6 | Includes accessibility/fairness standards plus specialist form-gap material for contemporary/physical strands |

**High-priority placement rationale**
- **ACTING-B1** is intentionally largest because later synthesis will need official admissions evidence before any practitioner or pedagogy language is allowed to influence acting-rubric development.
- **ACTING-B2** is essential for avoiding one generic acting standard; it is where screen/self-tape, eyeline, frame, text-type and speech-delivery evidence will likely concentrate.
- **ACTING-B3** remains smaller because professional guidance is valuable for process and output language, but it should not dominate descriptor logic over admissions and formal frameworks.
- **ACTING-B4** is deliberately protected for accessibility, anti-bias, method-neutral clarification and undercovered form areas. citeturn26search0turn28search0turn28search9turn26search1turn29search1turn31search3turn31search0

**Sources that could fit more than one batch**
- **Equity self-tape & Zoom guidance (ACTING-S035)** could sit in B3 or B4; it is placed in **B3** because its core value is professional process guidance, with accessibility crossover explicitly noted.
- **RADA self-tape guide (ACTING-S033)** could sit in B1 or B2; it is placed in **B2** because the extraction need is self-tape readability rather than admissions sequencing.
- **East 15 specialised acting courses (ACTING-S042–S043)** could sit in B1 or B4; they are placed in **B4** because they are form-specific gap-fill rather than core acting admissions anchors.

## 6. Source Alias / Normalisation Notes

- **Do not double-count Spotlight performer guides.**  
  ACTING-S034 is the preferred source family for Spotlight’s performer self-tape workflow. The represented-performer and self-represented-performer pages should be treated as one source family unless materially different criteria appear.
- **Do not double-count East 15 domain variants.**  
  `east15.ac.uk` and `www.east15.ac.uk` point to the same source family and should be normalised together.
- **Do not double-count Trinity legacy mirror pages.**  
  Prefer `trinitycollege.com` over older `www3.trinitycollege.com` mirrors.
- **Do not treat ACTING-S006 and ACTING-S007 as one source.**  
  ACTING-S006 is the unresolved current Royal Central admissions page group; ACTING-S007 is a fallback official guidance source and should not be treated as proof that the current admissions page has been verified.
- **Do not treat ACTING-S028 as an active admissions source.**  
  Drama Centre successor material was not confirmed; keep as contextual only.
- **RADA page family note.**  
  ACTING-S001 and ACTING-S033 belong to the same institution but are different documents; they may both matter later, but should not be double-counted as separate institutions.
- **Yale page family note.**  
  ACTING-S023 and ACTING-S024 are separate documents inside one programme source family; later extraction should preserve both because one covers application framing and the other covers live audition/callback structure.

## 7. Early Evidence-Gap Watchlist

This is **not** synthesis. It is an extraction watchlist only.

- Current official Royal Central acting admissions page.
- Screen acting self-tape criteria beyond general setup guidance.
- Stage acting versus screen naturalism descriptors.
- Classical / Shakespeare / heightened-text criteria.
- Contemporary text criteria.
- Comedy criteria.
- Physical-theatre / embodied-performance criteria.
- Monologue versus duologue / scene / reader-relationship criteria.
- Voice/speech delivery as acting evidence rather than singing.
- Tape-observable versus live-room-only criteria.
- Direction response / recall / workshop evidence.
- Methodology-neutral language for objective / action / tactic / beat / given circumstances.
- Accessibility-safe acting and speech assessment.
- Professional presentation versus appearance / class-coded polish.
- Role fit / brief handling without invented production-world expectations.
- Generic acting feedback suppression.

## 8. Reusable Handoff Pack for ACTING-B1

**ACTING-S0 handoff summary**

ACTING-S0 has established a usable public-web source universe for the next acting branch stage. Coverage is strongest in official drama-school and conservatoire admissions material, with especially solid current sources for RADA, LAMDA, Guildhall, Mountview, ArtsEd, East 15, Manchester School of Theatre, Oxford School of Drama, Royal Conservatoire of Scotland, Yale, Carnegie Mellon and USC. These sources should give ACTING-B1 a strong base for extracting audition structure, monologue requirements, self-tape instructions, recall/workshop processes, training-potential language and explicit statements about what panels are trying to assess. citeturn22search1turn37search3turn23search1turn22search3turn22search2turn24search5turn34search1turn35search0turn38search0turn25search0turn34search3turn34search0

Formal descriptor coverage is present and should be treated as a later anchor for acting domains and screen-specific language, primarily through LAMDA Exams and Trinity, including Trinity’s Acting for Screen materials. This should help later stages avoid collapsing stage, screen, monologue and duologue work into one generic acting standard. Professional-process and accessibility coverage is also already good enough to support later work on self-tape fairness, assessability, reader expectations, turnaround, accessible auditions and anti-deficit language, especially through Equity, SAG-AFTRA, ScreenSkills and Graeae. citeturn26search0turn28search0turn28search9turn26search1turn29search1turn31search3turn31search0

The main unresolved items are narrow rather than branch-blocking: the current public Royal Central acting admissions page was not confidently verified in this run; Drama Centre has no confirmed current successor material; and comedy / physical-theatre-specific formal criteria remain thinner than monologue, self-tape and classical/contemporary coverage. Those should be carried as explicit watch items into later extraction, not silently ignored.

\f0\b\fs36 \cf0 17. Reusable Handoff Pack for ACTING-REV\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\fs28 \cf0 ACTING-AUDIT handoff summary\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f1\b0\fs24 \cf0 The Acting audit is complete. The current Run 0B Acting baseline is directionally sound but still too generic and too shared-schema-shaped to be revision-ready without additional wording and guardrails. Its strongest existing features are that it already centres Acting, recognises speech/voice as distinct from singing, names useful acting behaviours such as intention, listening, eyeline, reader relationship, thought shifts and pacing, and warns not to invent role expectations where no brief exists. However, ACTING-SYN shows that Acting cannot remain one undifferentiated standard. The revision must now make monologue, scene/duologue, screen/self-tape, stage, classical/heated text and contemporary text handling explicit inside the current framework.\
The highest-priority audit issue is the reused 
\f2\fs26 vocal
\f1\fs24  field. The baseline correctly says spoken-only work should be labelled as speech delivery rather than vocal performance, but ACTING-REV must strengthen that into a clear user-facing label boundary: spoken Acting must not be described as singing or vocal performance unless singing is actually present. Closely linked is the need to separate speech audibility from speech skill.\
The second major priority is claim scope. Finished tapes can show text handling, speech clarity, camera relationship, visible choices, reader-mediated response and some physical evidence, but they cannot safely prove response to direction, group work, workshop behaviour, training potential or broader flexibility unless such evidence is directly shown or the context is admissions/live-stage. Reader availability, paid-reader quality, self-tape workload, production polish and equipment quality must also be treated as process or assessability issues, not acting merit.\
The third priority is accessibility-safe assessment. ACTING-REV must add explicit non-deficit handling for access needs, visual impairment, speech difference, mobility difference, interpreters, access workers, accessible materials, extra preparation and adaptation. These are process supports, not talent deficits.\
No backend, schema, score-field, weighting, cap, verdict or MT-stabilised-flow changes are supported. Physical/fight acting and comedy remain evidence-limited and should be carried as cautions rather than solved as universal rubrics.\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa280\partightenfactor0

\f0\b\fs36 \cf0 \strokec2 3. Final Audit Scope and Preservation Rules\
\pard\pardeftab720\sa240\partightenfactor0

\f1\b0\fs24 \cf0 This final audit covers whether the Acting revision package is materially responsive to ACTING-SYN-F01\'96F17 and ACTING-AUDIT-R01\'96R16, whether it preserves the current TapeCoach architecture, and whether it is ready to move to Acting Output Specificity / Non-Regression Test Mapping.\
It does not cover live rendered outputs, frontend label helpers, comparison-page label behaviour, renderer/export timestamp count, score recomputation code, schema implementation, production subtype extraction or product implementation.\
The following remain out of scope: backend changes, schema changes, field renames, score-field additions, weighting changes, cap/blocker/verdict changes, role-fit bound changes, pipeline changes, Step 1 / Step 2 rewrites and any change to the stabilised Musical Theatre acting + song flow.\
A return to ACTING-REV would be required only if the revised text introduced a schema/weighting change, failed to contain the spoken voice label risk, collapsed Acting into one generic standard, allowed access needs as deficits, imported external marks/methodologies as weights, or failed to ring-fence live-room capacities. None of those blocking failures are present.\
\pard\pardeftab720\partightenfactor0
\cf3 \strokec3 \
\pard\pardeftab720\sa298\partightenfactor0
